articles.title: How to build a simple skin care routine in Sri Lanka
articles.meta_title: Simple Skin Care Routine for Sri Lanka | Iconic Journal
articles.meta_desc: A four-step skin care routine for Sri Lanka's heat and humidity: cleanser, treatment, moisturiser and sunscreen, with patch-test and storage tips.
articles.excerpt: A four-step routine that works with Sri Lanka's heat and humidity, plus how to introduce a new product without changing everything at once.
articles.intro: A simple routine is easier to keep than a ten-step one. In Sri Lanka's heat and humidity, the aim is to cleanse gently, treat one concern, moisturise and protect your skin from the sun. This sample guide explains the order and the questions to ask before adding a new product.

p: Use a gentle cleanser in the morning and evening. If your skin feels tight after washing, the cleanser may be too strong or you may be washing for too long.
Follow with one treatment for your main concern, then a moisturiser. In the morning, finish with sunscreen. A separate night cream is optional; a moisturiser you already tolerate is usually enough.

In humid weather, a lighter lotion or gel may feel more comfortable than a rich cream. In air-conditioned rooms, you may prefer a slightly richer formula. Adjust by how your skin feels, not by the label alone.

sections.h: Introduce one product at a time
p: Add one new product every two weeks so you can tell whether it suits you. Patch-test a small area first, especially if you have reacted to products before.
If a product stings, burns or causes a rash, stop using it and check the pack. If the reaction is severe or does not settle, seek medical advice.
Keep products in a cool, dry place away from direct sun. Close lids properly and avoid leaving creams or serums in a hot car or on a sunny windowsill.
Check the pack for a period-after-opening symbol and follow it. If the texture, smell or colour changes, stop using the product.

takeaways: Cleanse gently, treat one concern, moisturise and use sunscreen in the morning.
Add one new product every two weeks and patch-test first.
Store products away from heat and direct sun, and check the pack for opening dates.

faqs.q: Do I need a separate morning and night routine?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Many people use the same gentle cleanser and moisturiser twice a day, with sunscreen added in the morning. A treatment may be used once a day at first. Check the pack for how often the product is intended to be used.

faqs.q: How long should I wait before judging a new product?
faqs.a: Give a new product two to four weeks of regular use before deciding, unless you have irritation. If you react, stop and check the pack. A patch test on a small area can help you spot a problem earlier.

No. A short routine you can follow consistently is usually easier to judge and maintain. Start with cleanse, treat, moisturise and sunscreen, then add a product only when you have a specific reason to do so.

articles.title: How to choose a foundation shade without guessing
articles.meta_title: How to Choose a Foundation Shade | Iconic Journal
articles.meta_desc: How to match a foundation shade: check undertone, test along the jawline, use natural light, watch for oxidation and ask for help when the shade is unclear.
articles.excerpt: A practical way to narrow down a foundation shade using undertone, jawline testing, natural light and a little patience.
articles.intro: Foundation is one of the hardest products to buy without testing. The shade on a screen, in a shop light and on your skin can all look different. This sample guide walks through a simple way to narrow the choice before you buy.

sections.h: Start with undertone, not just depth
p: Two shades can look equally light or deep but sit on different undertones. Compare a few swatches next to each other on your jawline rather than on your hand.
If a shade looks pink or orange against your neck, it is probably the wrong undertone even if the depth looks close.
Shop lighting can make a shade look cooler or warmer than it is. Take a photo in daylight or step near a window before deciding.
Some foundations look slightly different after they dry. Apply a thin layer, wait a few minutes and check the colour again before committing.

sections.h: Ask for help when you are between shades
p: If you are between two shades, ask which one the brand recommends for your undertone and finish. A sample or a small size is a lower-risk way to test at home.
Check the returns or exchange terms before opening a full-size product. This demo store does not sell or ship products, so use the contact form for a live-order question.

takeaways: Compare shades on the jawline, not the back of the hand.
Check the colour in daylight and after it dries.
Ask for help or a sample when you are between two shades.

faqs.q: Should foundation match my neck or my face?
faqs.a: Match the jawline and neck so the transition looks natural. If your face is slightly different in colour from your neck, test along the jaw and blend downward. Check the result in daylight rather than under shop lighting.

faqs.q: Why does foundation look different after a few minutes?
faqs.a: Some formulas change slightly as they dry or mix with your skin's natural oils. Apply a thin layer, wait a few minutes and check the colour again. If it turns noticeably orange or grey, try a different undertone.

faqs.q: Can I return a foundation if the shade is wrong?
faqs.a: That depends on the retailer and whether the product has been opened. Check the returns terms before buying, and ask for a sample or small size when possible. This demo store does not sell or ship products.

articles.title: Baby bath time: what to check on the pack
articles.meta_title: Baby Bath Time Checklist | Iconic Beauty & Baby Journal
articles.meta_desc: A simple baby bath-time checklist: check age guidance, read the pack, prepare the room, test the water temperature and never leave a baby unattended.
articles.excerpt: A calm bath-time checklist for parents and carers, focused on age guidance, pack directions, water temperature and supervision.
articles.intro: Baby bath products are not all the same. Age guidance, directions and warnings vary by product, so the pack is the first place to check. This sample guide covers the practical steps around bath time; it is not medical advice.

p: Some washes, oils and lotions are intended for a particular age range. Read the front and back of the pack before using a new product on a baby or toddler.
If the pack does not state an age range, ask the brand or your health visitor before using it. Do not assume a product is suitable because it is sold in the baby aisle.

sections.h: Prepare the room and the water
p: Have everything you need within reach before you start: towel, clean clothes, nappy and any product you plan to use. Test the water with your wrist or elbow; it should feel comfortably warm, not hot.
Never leave a baby or young child unattended in the bath, even for a moment. Keep one hand on the child and keep the room warm enough to avoid chilling.

sections.h: Use only what the pack recommends
p: Follow the amount and directions on the pack. More product is not better, and some washes need to be diluted. Rinse carefully and pat the skin dry rather than rubbing.
If a product causes redness, dryness or irritation, stop using it and check the pack. If the reaction is severe or does not settle, seek medical advice.

takeaways: Read the age guidance and directions on the pack before use.
Prepare everything first and test the water temperature.
Never leave a baby unattended in the bath.

faqs.q: Can I use adult body wash on a baby?
faqs.a: No. Adult washes can be too fragranced or drying for a baby's skin. Use a product intended for the child's age and follow the pack directions. If you are unsure, ask your health visitor or doctor before using it.

faqs.q: How warm should a baby's bath be?
faqs.a: The water should feel comfortably warm, not hot. Test it with your wrist or elbow and mix it well so there are no hot spots. Keep the room warm and have a towel ready before the bath starts.

faqs.q: What should I do if a bath product irritates the skin?
faqs.a: Stop using the product, rinse the skin with clean water and check the pack. If the irritation is severe, spreading or does not settle, seek medical advice. Keep the pack or a photo of the label so you can check the ingredients.

articles.title: How to store perfume and makeup in a hot, humid climate
articles.meta_title: Store Perfume & Makeup in Heat | Iconic Journal
articles.meta_desc: How to store perfume and makeup in Sri Lanka's heat and humidity: keep products cool and dark, close lids, avoid the bathroom shelf and watch for texture changes.
articles.excerpt: Small storage changes that help perfume, creams and makeup stay in better condition in heat and humidity.
articles.intro: Heat, light and humidity can change how a product looks, smells and feels. You do not need a special fridge or a dedicated beauty cupboard; a few simple storage habits are enough for most products.

sections.h: Keep products cool and out of direct sun
p: A closed drawer or cupboard away from a window is usually better than a sunny shelf. Avoid leaving perfume or makeup in a hot car, even for a short time.
Some products are fine at room temperature. Check the pack for any specific storage instructions before moving them somewhere colder or warmer.

sections.h: Close lids and keep water out
p: Close cream, serum and perfume lids properly after use. Water getting into a jar can change the texture and make it more likely to spoil.
A steamy bathroom is not the best long-term home for products that are sensitive to humidity. If you store makeup there, keep it in a closed bag or box.

sections.h: Watch for changes and respect opening dates
p: Check the pack for a period-after-opening symbol and follow it. If a product changes colour, separates, smells different or feels gritty, stop using it.
Keep applicators and brushes clean and avoid sharing products that touch broken skin or eyes. When in doubt, replace the product rather than trying to revive it.

takeaways: Store products in a cool, dark place away from direct sun.
Close lids tightly and keep water out of creams and serums.
Check opening dates and stop using a product if its texture or smell changes.

faqs.q: Should I keep perfume in the fridge?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. A cool, dark cupboard is usually enough. If you do use a fridge, keep the bottle sealed and away from food, and check the pack for any storage instructions. Avoid repeated temperature changes.

faqs.q: Can I use makeup that has changed texture?
faqs.a: If a product has separated, dried out, changed colour or smells different, stop using it. Check the pack for a period-after-opening symbol. Replacing it is safer than trying to mix it back into shape.

faqs.q: Why does my cream feel different in humid weather?
faqs.a: Humidity and heat can change how a cream feels on the skin and how quickly it absorbs. Store it as directed on the pack, close the lid properly and check for any change in texture or smell before using it.
